title: Why You Must Be Relentlessly Honest With Students
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin builds a list of common teacher gaps between stated standards and actual practice -- having rules but not always following them, preaching kindness without practicing it, accepting late work despite deadlines, promising interesting lessons without delivering -- and argues that from a student's perspective, these aren't minor oversights but outright lies, regardless of how adults rationalize them. He walks through seven specific consequences of this perceived dishonesty (loss of trust, attentiveness, leadership standing, respect, presence, influence, and even credibility of the content being taught), arguing each one compounds the others until a teacher's words carry no real weight. He specifically rejects the common adult assumption that kids either won't notice or will tacitly accept 'how the game works,' calling this a fundamental misreading of what drives student behavior, and argues the stakes are especially high now. The piece ends on an optimistic note, though, insisting students are quick to forgive and recalibrate once a teacher becomes genuinely honest, transparent, and reliable.
points: What adults dismiss as oversights or 'white lies' (unenforced rules, accepted late work, undelivered promises) register to students as outright lies.
Perceived dishonesty compounds across seven areas -- trust, attentiveness, leadership, respect, presence, influence, and even credibility of the lessons themselves.
Rejects the common belief that students won't notice or will tacitly accept adult inconsistency as 'how the game works.'
Students are quick to forgive and recalibrate their trust once a teacher becomes consistently honest, transparent, and reliable.
quotes: To an adult, they may not seem blatant or purposeful or to even rise to the level of real lies. I’ve heard teachers describe them as oversights, mistakes, or white lies.
To students they’re bald-faced. They’re obvious, predictable, and shameless. This is all that matters. Thus, engaging in them, as many teachers are wont to do, is a huge mistake.
If you say you’ll do something and don’t do it, then your students won’t trust you.
They think kids either won’t notice, won’t care, or “wink, wink” know how the game works.
The good news is that students are forgiving and will quickly adjust and turn the page. You can change today.
